question.:question/problem:
According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+1,\,{y}^{2}⟩$
across the triangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),$ and $(0,2)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/c3/c3c617522488e6ebf47dd2b2a52c43a1fe06ccaef8cd1e8752ab4df5e2d4bd64.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+1$ and $Q(x,y)={y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2(x+y).$

question.:question/problem:

$F(x,y)=\langle x^{2} + 1,y^{2}\rangle$
across the triangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),$ and $(0,2)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/c3/c3c617522488e6ebf47dd2b2a52c43a1fe06ccaef8cd1e8752ab4df5e2d4bd64.png)

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2 x,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=2 y .

$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2 \left(x + y\right).$

Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)=(9 x y^{3})\,i+(18 x y^{4})\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/fa/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=9 x y^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=18 x y^{4}.$ So,

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=9 y^{3},\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=72 x y^{3} .
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\ 0\le y\le 2\} .
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x &= \iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\text{d}A \\ &=\iint_D\left((9 y^{3})+(72 x y^{3})\right)\,\text{d}A \\ &=\int_{-1}^{1}\int_{0}^{2}9 y^{3} \left(8 x + 1\right)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
